newsitem.title: USA: Market reactions to data, Fed's remarks "inane" - Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Market reactions to data, Fed's remarks "inane" - Jordan.

text.p: Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank President Jerry Jordan on Thursday called financial market reactions to data and central bankers' remarks "inane."

Jordan described "market reactions to statistics and remarks by policymakers as being rather like the inane sports talk shows where people call in to debate whether or not it was really wise to run a ball play on third and long at that stage of the game last Sunday.
"Those things will be forgotten a week later," Jordan told a two-day conference on the "Dynamic Effects of Monetary Policy" sponsored by the Cleveland Fed.

Commenting on the relationship between monetary policy and the economy, Jordan singled out two main theories. "The first is that money is neutral in the long run ... (and) the second hypothesis is that money is not neutral in the short-run and has some transitional effect on the pace of real economic activity."

Jordan said a challenge is to reconcile the two views in a framework that is also useful to policy makers. He said it also may help "people who are unsure about the objectives of a central bank and may even not believe the statements of central bankers when they announce their intentions."
Turning to the current state of U.S. monetary policy, Jordan noted the current debate centers around whether the Fed should target price stability or zero inflation.
"This is a nice problem to have," he added.

A number of senior Fed officials and academics taking part in the Cleveland Fed conference have authored papers about targeting the inflation rate or the nominal Gross Domestic Product as guides for monetary policy.
